nodes.title: OCIO Color Space - sRGB to scene-linear ACEScg
Note:
widgets_values:
My recommendation is to convert all sRGB inputs to Rec.709 before sending them into the LTX 2.5 model. This helps preserve detail near black instead of producing unclamped black patches.

You have two options:

1. Use the OCIO Color Space node, as shown here.
2. In the OCIO Read node, keep the input color space set to sRGB and change the output color space to Rec.709.

nodes.title: Note:
widgets_values:
Use the custom **OCIO VAE Decode** node directly after the LTX 2.5 model.

This node was designed specifically to produce unclamped, clean Float32 output. It preserves values above 1.0 and, just as importantly, negative values below 0. These values are necessary for professional, scene-referred color workflows used in the film industry.

The node does not output sRGB. It outputs the same color space that was supplied to LTX 2.5, in this case Rec.709.

For this reason, set **From Color Space** to **Rec.709**, not sRGB. Otherwise, the image will appear darker.

This preserves the same color and tone as the input, but now in full range, with more available stops and higher lighting precision.

nodes.title: Note:
widgets_values:
There is one small tradeoff with this method.

If you want harder, brighter highlights, do not convert the input to Rec.709 before LTX 2.5. Send it into the model as **sRGB**.

Then, in the already connected **OCIO Write** node, set `From_ColorSpace` to **sRGB** instead of Rec.709.

The tradeoff is that some detail in the darker areas will be lost.

Lifehack:
When working in sRGB, try lifting the black point slightly above zero. This gives LTX 2.5 information in the darkest areas, so it can generate detail there instead of treating them as empty black patches.

nodes.title: OCIO LogConvert - Linear to ACEScct (model input)
OCIO LogConvert - ACEScct to Linear (model output)
OCIO Write - ACEScct probe, linear EXR 32f
Note: what this probe tests, and what it found
widgets_values:
## What this graph tests, and what it found

Lightricks describe LTX-2.5 as having **native 4K HDR**. In their reference CLI
(`Lightricks/LTX-2`) that is reached with `--hdr {SRGB_LINEAR,ACESCG,ACESCCT}`, and reading
`ltx_pipelines/utils/media_io/color_config.py` the flag does three things and no more: it declares
the source colour space, decodes the VAE in float32 instead of bf16, and sets the writer.
**It loads no extra weights and selects no other checkpoint.** Scene-linear input is compressed
through **ACEScct** on load, so in HDR mode the model works in ACEScct codes.

This graph builds the same shape here, which ComfyUI cannot otherwise do:
`sRGB -> ACEScg -> Linear to Log (ACEScct) -> LTX-2.5 -> decode -> Log to Linear (ACEScct) -> EXR 32f`.

### The answer: 0.08 of a stop

Measured 2026-08-17 at 1280x704 on a deliberately punishing scene - a figure leaving a dark cave onto
a sunlit ocean, sun flaring into the lens. **Convert the picture properly first**, then apply exposure:
undo the write's Rec.709 to AP1 matrix, recover the model's display codes, take BT.1886 to linear, and
only then step the exposure.

Result: **2.21% of samples above diffuse white, peak 1.0544** - eight hundredths of a stop of headroom.
Step down and the sun is gone by -4 EV, where real HDR would still hold a disc at -10. Downward range is
genuine: at +4 EV the cave rock still carries texture, so shadows are not crushed.

### Why the same frames can look like eleven stops

Apply the ladder *before* that conversion, straight on the ACEScct-decoded values, and the same file
reads as 11.5 stops with a peak of 368. Both numbers are arithmetically correct; they differ only in
where the ladder was applied. The earlier reading measures the curve, not the picture.

A second check says the same thing. ACEScct codes diffuse white at `0.5548`, so under that reading
**30.5% of the frame claims to be brighter than white paper in sunlight**. A lit exterior puts 1-10%
there. Read as display, the same pixels put 0.55% above white, which is ordinary.

**Conclusion: LTX-2.5 emits codes distributed like an ordinary display picture. Reading them as ACEScct
stretches the range rather than revealing one.**

### Two traps this graph documents

**Primaries.** `OCIO LogConvert` undoes a transfer curve only; it never moves primaries. What goes in
comes out in the same primaries - Rec.709 on this path - so the write's `input_colorspace` must say
`Linear Rec.709 (sRGB)`, not `ACEScg`. Getting that wrong makes the write a no-op and leaves Rec.709
numbers in a file labelled ACEScg: measured at +20% chroma with red high by 10.5%, luminance almost
unchanged. It looks like a grade, not a bug.

**Bypass.** Switching to text-to-video sets `bypass` on `LTXV Img To Video Inplace`, and
`comfy_extras/nodes_lt.py` then does `if bypass: return (latent,)` - the input image, and any colour
conversion in front of it, is skipped entirely. In that mode the curve only ever touches the output.

### Level, versus the LTX-2.5 graph

This graph's write uses `view = (none) colorimetric, no tone map`. The LTX-2.5 graph's EXR write uses
`view = ACES 1.3: ACES 1.0 - SDR Video`, which inverts the ACES output transform. Both are called
scene-linear and both are legitimate, but they are calibrated differently: measured on one run, the
ratio is 3.4x in the shadows and 0.81x at p99, so no single exposure offset makes them match. Expect
roughly 1.3-1.5 stops darker at mid grey here. It is a different curve, not a different level.

The three original writes and the player are **muted, not deleted** - they read the decode as
Rec.1886/Rec.709 display, which is not what leaves the model on this path.

nodes.title: Note: level and primaries vs the LTX-2.5 graph
widgets_values:
## Reading these EXRs next to the LTX-2.5 ones

The scene-linear write in this graph uses `view = (none) colorimetric, no tone map`: the values are
carried by a colour transform and nothing else. The LTX-2.5 graph's EXR write
(`OCIO_WORKFLOW_LTX_2.5.json`, the `$OUTPUT/EXR_SEQ` node) instead uses
`view = ACES 1.3: ACES 1.0 - SDR Video`, which **inverts** the ACES output transform to get back to
scene-linear.

Both are legitimate and both are called scene-linear, but they are calibrated differently, so the two
sequences will not sit at the same level. Measured on one run, same scene, 25 frames:

| quantile | ACES-inverted write | colorimetric write | ratio |
|---|---|---|---|
| p1 | 0.00542 | 0.00161 | 3.36 |
| p50 | 0.08341 | 0.03348 | 2.49 |
| p90 | 0.34212 | 0.24907 | 1.37 |
| p99 | 2.96199 | 3.67842 | 0.81 |

The ratio is not constant - 3.4x in the shadows, 0.8x at p99 - so **no single exposure offset makes
them match**. It is a different curve, not a different level. Expect roughly 1.3-1.5 stops darker at
mid grey here, and grade accordingly rather than treating it as a fault.

Which one to prefer: this one is the physical answer, because the curve was undone by the transform
that encoded it. The ACES-inverted one is the practical answer for SDR generations, where no encoded
curve exists to undo. Pick per shot, and keep one choice across a sequence.

**Primaries matter as much as the curve.** `OCIO LogConvert` undoes a transfer curve only; it never
moves primaries. Whatever went in comes out in the same primaries, which on these paths is Rec.709 -
so the write's `input_colorspace` must say `Linear Rec.709 (sRGB)`, not `ACEScg`. Getting that wrong
makes the write a no-op and leaves Rec.709 numbers in a file labelled ACEScg: measured at +20% chroma
and red high by 10.5%, with luminance almost unchanged, which is exactly the kind of error that looks
like a grade rather than a bug.

nodes.title: Note: sRGB for text-to-video, Rec.709 for image-to-video
widgets_values:
## Set the display colorspace by what you fed the model

This graph ships wired for **image-to-video**, where `OCIO Color Space` converts the input plate
`sRGB - Display` -> `Rec.1886 Rec.709 - Display` before the model. Because the input was converted,
the output is read back the same way: every node downstream that treats the decode as a display
signal is set to `Rec.1886 Rec.709 - Display`.

**Switch to text-to-video and that stops being true.** There is no input plate, so no conversion
happens, and the model emits its own native, sRGB-like signal. Every display colorspace on the
output side must then say `sRGB - Display`:

| node | image-to-video | text-to-video |
|---|---|---|
| `OCIO Write` (ProRes) in/out | `Rec.1886 Rec.709 - Display` | `sRGB - Display` |
| `OCIO Write` (EXR) input | `Rec.1886 Rec.709 - Display` | `sRGB - Display` |
| `OCIO Player` in/out | `Rec.1886 Rec.709 - Display` | `sRGB - Display` |
| any `OCIO Color Space` reading the decode | `Rec.1886 Rec.709 - Display` | `sRGB - Display` |

Linear colorspaces are unaffected: `Linear Rec.709 (sRGB)` already names both, because Rec.709 and
sRGB share primaries and differ only in transfer.

**What it costs to get wrong.** Measured on a text-to-video run read as Rec.1886 instead of sRGB, the
sequence needed x8.52 to reach mid grey where the reference needed x2.97 - about 1.5 stops adrift, and
it looks like a grading problem rather than a settings one. Read correctly as sRGB the same pair came
out at x1.21 and x0.96, which is a match.

`bypass` on `LTXV Img To Video Inplace` is what makes the graph text-to-video: their code does
`if bypass: return (latent,)` (`comfy_extras/nodes_lt.py`), so the input image and every colour
conversion in front of it are skipped entirely.

nodes.title: Which weights this graph loads, and why the CLI needs different ones
widgets_values:
# Which weights this graph loads, and why the CLI needs different ones

There are two ways to reach ACEScct with LTX-2.5, and **they do not load the same files.**

## This graph, running inside ComfyUI

| slot | file | size |
| --- | --- | --- |
| transformer | `ltx-2.5-22b-distilled-transformer-comfy-int8-convrot.safetensors` | 20.03 GiB |
| text encoder | `gemma4-12b-with-proj-ltx-2.5-comfy-int8-convrot.safetensors` | 14.32 GiB |
| video VAE | `ltx-2.5-video-vae-bf16.safetensors` | 1.37 GiB |
| audio VAE | `ltx-2.5-audio-vae-bf16.safetensors` | 0.34 GiB |
| latent upscaler | `ltx-2.5-latent-spatial-upscaler-x2-bf16-1.0.safetensors` | 0.93 GiB |

The two large ones are the INT8 `comfy-int8-convrot` builds, quantised for ComfyUI. About
34 GiB in total.

## Lightricks' own CLI, which is where the `--hdr ACESCCT` flag lives

The same VAEs and the same upscaler, but the transformer and the text encoder must be the
**bf16** builds: `ltx-2.5-22b-distilled-transformer-bf16.safetensors` at 39.13 GiB and
`gemma4-12b-with-proj-ltx-2.5-bf16.safetensors` at 24.46 GiB. About 64 GiB in total.

**This is not a preference.** Their CLI does not recognise the `convrot` checkpoints: the
string appears nowhere in their source. Pointing it at the files this graph uses does not work.

## So what is this graph, exactly

It builds the SHAPE of their native HDR path inside ComfyUI: sRGB in, converted to ACEScg,
compressed to ACEScct codes before the model, and decompressed after it. That is measurable
and it is what the notes elsewhere in this graph record.

It is **not** the same thing as running their `--hdr ACESCCT` pipeline. That one does the
compression internally, keeps the VAE in float32, and writes EXR frames tagged ACEScct plus a
BT.2020 HLG master. Reaching it means their CLI, their bf16 weights, and no ComfyUI.

Measured on one shot through their CLI, for reference: the plate encoded to ACEScct had a code
median of 0.3295, and their output came back at 0.3298, so the level is preserved. Decoded to
linear that output peaks at 71.38, and code 1.0 in ACEScct is 222.9 linear against 55.1 for
the ARRI LogC3 curve the LTX-2.3 HDR IC-LoRA path is fixed to.
